title: False Friends Ambush
intro: Embarazada isn’t embarrassed. Actualmente isn’t actually. The words that look Spanish and betray you every time — match each one to what it really means.

A2.right: self-conscious and awkward, red in the face
A2.why: Embarrassed means self-conscious and awkward; Spanish “embarazada” is “pregnant”, a classic and very public mistake.

A2.right: a place where you borrow books
A2.why: You borrow books from a library; a shop that sells them, Spanish “librería”, is a “bookshop”.

A2.right: a thick covering for a floor
A2.why: A carpet goes on the floor; your papers go in a “folder”, Spanish “carpeta”.

A2.right: the way out of a building
A2.why: Exit is the door out; Spanish “éxito” is “success”.
Large means big, as in a large ranch; Spanish “largo” is “long”.

A2.right: to act as if something is true when it isn't
A2.why: The outlaw pretended to be a priest; Spanish “pretender” (to aim or intend) is “intend” or “try to”.
Actually means in fact; Spanish “actualmente” is “currently” or “at the moment”.

A2.right: to suddenly understand or become aware of something
A2.why: Realise means understand suddenly; Spanish “realizar” (a task) is “carry out” or “do”.
Success is a good result; Spanish “suceso”, an incident in the news, is an “incident” or “event”.
Once means one time, as in “I’ve been to Toledo once”; Spanish “once” is “eleven”.

A2.right: a metal container for cooking on the hob
A2.why: A paella is cooked in a pan; Spanish “pan” is “bread”.

A2.right: the elected head of a town or city
A2.why: The mayor runs the town hall; Spanish “mayor” is “older” or “elder”.

B1.why: Assist means help; Spanish “asistir” (to go to an event) is “attend”.

B1.right: kind and understanding when someone is suffering
B1.why: Sympathetic means kind when someone is suffering; Spanish “simpático” is “nice” or “friendly”.
A sensible person makes wise choices; Spanish “sensible” is “sensitive”.

B1.right: unable to empty your bowels easily
B1.why: Constipated is about your bowels; Spanish “constipado” is “a cold”, a mistake to avoid at the doctor’s.
An argument is a quarrel; Spanish “argumento” (of a film or book) is the “plot”.

B1.right: the series of jobs you do over your working life
B1.why: A career is your working life; Spanish “carrera” (at university) is a “degree” or “degree course”.

B1.right: real, as opposed to imagined or expected
B1.why: Actual means real, as in the actual cost; Spanish “actual” (present-day) is “current”.

B1.right: in the end, after a long time
B1.why: Eventually means in the end; Spanish “eventualmente” is “possibly” or “if necessary”.
Misery is deep unhappiness; Spanish “miseria” is usually “poverty”, and a tiny amount is “a pittance”.
Bland food has little taste; Spanish “blando” is “soft”.

B1.right: to start again after a pause
B1.why: The meeting resumed after lunch; Spanish “resumir” is “summarise”.

B1.right: a senior teacher at a university
B1.why: Only senior university staff are professors; Spanish “profesor” also covers school teachers, who are “teachers”.

B2.right: an agreement where both sides give something up
B2.why: A compromise is a deal where both sides give a little; Spanish “compromiso” is usually a “commitment” or an “engagement”.

B2.right: a strong feeling that something is revolting
B2.why: Disgust is strong revulsion; Spanish “disgusto” (being upset) is “upset” or “annoyance”.

B2.right: to abuse someone sexually (a very serious word)
B2.why: Molest is a very serious word; for Spanish “molestar” say “bother” or “disturb”.

B2.right: a formal talk to an audience, often at university
B2.why: A lecture is a formal talk; Spanish “lectura” is “reading”.

B2.right: cloth used to make clothes or curtains
B2.why: Fabric is cloth; Spanish “fábrica” is a “factory”.
Sane means mentally healthy; Spanish “sano” (healthy in general) is “healthy”.

B2.right: the act of tricking or lying to people
B2.why: Deception means tricking people; Spanish “decepción” is “disappointment”.

B2.right: having had a good schooling, knowledgeable
B2.why: Educated means well schooled; Spanish “educado” is “polite” or “well-mannered”.

B2.right: eager and enthusiastic about something good
B2.why: “I’m excited about the trip” is completely normal English; Spanish “excitado” suggests agitated or even sexually aroused.
A rare stamp is hard to find; Spanish “raro” is “strange” or “odd”.

B2.right: a subject to talk or write about
B2.why: A topic is a subject; Spanish “tópico” is a “cliché” or “stereotype”, like paella and flamenco for every Spaniard.
A quiet room has little noise; Spanish “¡Estate quieto!” is “Keep still!”.

C1.right: in the end, when everything is considered
C1.why: Ultimately means in the end; Spanish “últimamente” is “lately” or “recently”.

C1.right: a fixed expression whose meaning is not literal
C1.why: An idiom is a fixed expression like “bite the bullet”; Spanish “idioma” is a “language”.

C1.right: separate and distinct from each other
C1.why: Discrete parts are separate; tactful, Spanish “discreto”, is “discreet”, spelt differently.
Gracious means polite and generous; Spanish “gracioso” is “funny”.

C1.right: a person injured or killed in an accident or war
C1.why: Casualties are people hurt or killed; Spanish “casualidad” is a “coincidence” or “chance”.

C1.right: a company, especially of lawyers or accountants
C1.why: A law firm is a company; your handwritten name, Spanish “firma”, is your “signature”.

C1.right: an expression of regret for something you did
C1.why: An apology means saying sorry; Spanish “apología” (a defence of something) is a “defence” or “justification”.

C1.right: the natural colour and texture of the skin on your face
C1.why: A pale complexion is about your facial skin; Spanish “complexión” (body build) is “build”.
Intoxicated means drunk; Spanish “intoxicado” means “poisoned”, as in “intoxicación alimentaria”, food poisoning.

C1.right: to avoid giving a direct answer
C1.why: A politician who prevaricates dodges the question; Spanish “prevaricar” means an official knowingly making an unjust decision.
The town greeted the news with jubilation; Spanish “jubilación” is “retirement”.

C1.right: a supporter of the arts, or a regular customer
C1.why: The Medici were patrons of the arts; Spanish “patrón” (at work) is a “boss” or “employer”, though “santo patrón” really is a “patron saint”.
